extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, publishers, research-integrity professionals, and policymakers interested in publication fraud and research integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and recommended practices for detecting, preventing, and responding to coordinated publication fraud (paper mills, brokers, predatory publishers) across journals, conferences, and databases. Covers institutional/publisher actions, detection signals, data sources, and individual-level responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global stakeholder coordination and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “We need the biggest, most important stakeholders of science to come together to talk about what needs to be done, what standards need to be implemented and not wait for the problem to solve itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for national academies and major science organizations to implement and advocate decisions that journals, funders, employers, and institutions must adopt; emphasizes coordinated action rather than relying on individual choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change research incentives / end hyper-competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should "press on policymakers to end the culture of hyper-competition in science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to alter incentive structures (hiring, funding, promotion, residency requirements) that drive researchers toward quantity-focused outputs that fuel demand for paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication screening of papers, authors, and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should "thoroughly screen new papers, authors and editors before publication."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes vetting author identities/affiliations, checking editor handling practices, and applying editorial checks before acceptance; PLOS and IEEE cited such preventive measures as essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate existing articles and paper-mill networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should implement measures "to investigate existing articles and paper mill networks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively review back-catalogue content for signs of coordinated fraud, not just screening new submissions; expand publication-ethics teams to examine networks and clusters of suspect articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: publish handling editor names and allow bulk access/Open Access
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of PLOS data was possible because PLOS "publishes all of our articles Open Access, we list the names of handling editors on our articles, and we allow bulk access to our article content and metadata."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages journals to increase transparency (disclose handling editors, enable bulk metadata access, open access) to enable independent analyses of editorial networks and patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor editor networks for abnormal acceptance/retraction rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify networks of editors who accepted an abnormally high rate of papers that were later retracted or flagged for concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure each editor's share of all articles vs. share of retracted/flagged articles (example: 45 editors edited 1.3% of articles but 30.2% of retracted articles); flag editors whose acceptance patterns deviate from norms for further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple data sources to detect patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine metadata and databases such as Scopus, Clarivate’s Web of Science, Retraction Watch Database, PubPeer comments, DOIs and publisher metadata to map networks and detect clusters of problematic publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulate across data sources (publisher metadata, indexing databases, crowdsourced comments) to improve detection coverage and reduce false positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect image-duplication networks and other clustered signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze image duplication networks — mapping duplicated images across papers — to find clusters that suggest coordinated activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors' approach of looking at image duplication networks is noted as innovative; such analyses can reveal multiple clusters of duplicated images published close in time and across publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tortured phrases and instrument misidentification as rare signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use "rare signals, like the comments that people leave on PubPeer observations about image misidentification and image duplication and instrument misidentification, tortured phrases … to understand what's happening behind the scenes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated or manual scanning for hallmark textual artifacts ("tortured phrases"), instrument/microscope misidentification, and other oddities can be effective heuristics for flagging suspect papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop high-throughput automated detection approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should develop "high throughput approaches to identify problematic articles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages creation and deployment of scalable computational tools and pipelines (textual analysis, image forensics, metadata anomaly detection) to triage large volumes of literature for manual follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and crowdsourced flagging
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals can "do post-publication peer review, and take a critical eye to the literature" and contribute via platforms like PubPeer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community-driven flagging and commentary are important corrective mechanisms; crowdsourced comments can be mined as signals for automated detection systems and for prioritizing investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retract suspected paper-mill products and de-index journals when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The study found only ~28.7% of suspected paper mill products have been retracted and extrapolated that only ~25% will ever be retracted; de-indexing of problematic journals is used as a response (e.g., journals listed by brokers were de-indexed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use retraction and de-indexing as corrective measures; monitor and consider removing journals from indexing services when systemic problems are identified to reduce the venues available to paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers should inspect their digital libraries and act appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers (e.g., IEEE) stated they "continuously inspects our digital library and acts accordingly when we become aware of possible issues with content, takes the appropriate level of care and time in our review, and, if necessary, retracts nonconforming publications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine audits of publisher archives, timely investigation of complaints, and clear workflows for retraction or correction are required; publishers should allocate resources and time to do this carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conference proceedings oversight and committee vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference series and their organizing committees can produce abnormally high proportions of problematic papers; seven IEEE conference series were flagged every year they were held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor conference series for repeat patterns, vet program committees/organizers, and consider flagging or blocking conferences with persistent high rates of suspect content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and quantify journal-hopping by brokers
rubrics_metrics.description: Track brokers' advertised journal lists and journal-hopping behavior as journals are de-indexed and brokers substitute new venues (example: ARDA listing journals it guaranteed publication in, which were then de-indexed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow brokers' public listings, compare to indexing status and retraction/de-indexing rates, and use that information to identify shifting networks of venues exploited by paper mills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require submission of raw analytical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary notes most fraud will never be detected because "journals don't require submission of raw analytical data."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandate submission and public availability (where appropriate) of raw data and underlying analyses as a preventive measure to facilitate verification and reproducibility; lacking data makes detection harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual-level assessment and de-funding of paper-mill outputs in hiring/selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to "don't cite authors who publish with papermills, don't subscribe to journals that publish papermill slop" and to perform due diligence when using publications as markers of researcher quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions, funders, and hiring committees should penalize or deprioritize CVs containing suspect publications, and individuals should avoid amplifying papermill outputs (citation, subscription, endorsement).
